subtopics.title: The atmosphere as a global system

outcomes.text: Explain how global atmospheric circulation cells and ocean currents move heat around the Earth.
Explain how circulation sets where arid (high pressure) and high rainfall (low pressure) areas lie.
Explain natural causes of past climate change: asteroid impacts, orbital changes, volcanoes, solar output.
Use ice cores, tree rings and historical sources to reconstruct past and UK climate.
Explain how human activities produce greenhouse gases that cause the enhanced greenhouse effect and warming.
Describe the evidence for human-caused climate change and its possible consequences for people.
Describe projections of temperature and sea-level change and why they are uncertain.
Describe tropical cyclones' characteristics, seasonal distribution, source areas and tracks.
Explain how global circulation produces tropical cyclones, why some intensify and how they dissipate.
Describe tropical cyclones' physical hazards and their impacts on people and environments.
Explain why some countries are more vulnerable to tropical cyclones than others.

subtopics.title: Preparing for and responding to cyclones

outcomes.text: Describe how countries prepare for and respond to tropical cyclones using forecasting, warning and defences.
Evaluate the effectiveness of preparation and response in one developed and one developing or emerging country.
Describe Earth's layers and their composition and physical properties.
Explain how the core's heat drives convection, the basis of plate tectonics.
Describe the distribution and characteristics of conservative, convergent and divergent boundaries and hotspots.
Explain the causes of contrasting volcanic and earthquake hazards, including tsunami.

subtopics.title: Impacts and management of tectonic hazards

outcomes.text: Compare primary and secondary impacts of an earthquake or volcano in a developed and a developing or emerging country.
Compare management of volcanic or earthquake hazards in a developed and a developing or emerging country.
Compare ways of defining and measuring development, such as GDP per capita, HDI and inequality measures.
Describe how demographic data differ between developing, emerging and developed countries.
Explain the social, historical, environmental, economic and political causes and consequences of global inequality.
Use Rostow's modernisation theory and Frank's dependency theory to explain development over time.
Describe top-down and bottom-up strategies and how TNCs and governments drive globalisation.
Evaluate NGO-led, intermediate technology, IGO-funded infrastructure and TNC investment approaches.
Explain the chosen emerging country's site, situation and connectivity in national, regional and global context.
Describe the country's political, social, cultural and environmental context.
Describe the country's key economic trends since 1990.
Explain the roles of globalisation and government policy in its development.
Explain how rapid growth caused demographic change, urbanisation and regional differences.
Assess positive and negative impacts of development on different age and gender groups.
Assess the environmental impacts of development at local to global scales.
Explain how rapid development changed the country's geopolitical influence and relations with the EU and USA.
Evaluate conflicting views on the costs and benefits of foreign investment and changing international relations.

units.title: Topic 3: Challenges of an urbanising world

topics.title: Rapid urbanisation and global urban trends

outcomes.text: Describe global urbanisation trends since 1980, regional variation and future projections.
Describe the pattern of megacities and urban primacy.
Explain how economic change and migration affect city growth or decline in different countries.
Explain why urban economies differ between developing, emerging and developed countries.
Describe how urban population and spatial growth change over time through urbanisation, suburbanisation, de-industrialisation and regeneration.
Describe urban land uses and the factors that influence them.
Explain the megacity's site, situation and connectivity in national, regional and global context.
Describe the megacity's structure (CBD, inner city, suburbs, rural-urban fringe) by function and building age.
Explain reasons for the megacity's population growth trends.
Explain how population growth changed spatial growth, functions and land use.

subtopics.title: Opportunities, challenges and quality of life

outcomes.text: Describe the opportunities for people living in the megacity.
Describe the challenges caused by rapid population growth.
Explain why quality of life differs within the megacity and the challenges of managing it.
Evaluate city-wide top-down strategies for a more sustainable megacity.
Evaluate community and NGO-led bottom-up strategies for sustainability.

units.title: Topic 4: The UK's evolving physical landscape

topics.title: Overview of the UK's physical landscape

outcomes.text: Explain how geology and past tectonic and glacial processes shaped upland and lowland landscapes.
Describe the characteristics and distribution of the UK's main rock types.
Explain how weathering, climate and post-glacial river and slope processes create distinctive landscapes.
Explain how agriculture, forestry and settlement have shaped distinctive landscapes.

subtopics.title: Coastal landscapes of erosion and deposition

outcomes.text: Explain how geological structure and rock type influence erosional coastal landforms.
Explain how climate, waves, weathering and mass movement shape erosional coasts and coastal retreat.
Explain how longshore drift and constructive waves form spits, beaches and bars.
Explain how development, farming, industry and coastal management affect coastal landscapes.
Explain how physical and human processes cause change on one named coastal landscape.
Explain the rising risks of coastal flooding and the threats to people and environment.
Evaluate hard, soft and sustainable coastal management options and the conflicting views on them.
Compare upper, middle and lower courses of a named UK river, including channel, valley and sediment changes.
Explain how erosion, transport and deposition form meanders, waterfalls, flood plains, levees and oxbow lakes.
Explain how climate, geology and slope processes affect rivers, and how storm hydrographs and lag times arise.
Explain how urbanisation, land-use change and deforestation alter river landscapes and hydrographs.
Explain how physical and human processes cause flooding on one named river.
Explain the increasing risks of river flooding and the threats to people and environment.
Evaluate the costs and benefits of hard and soft engineering flood management.

units.title: Topic 5: The UK's evolving human landscape

topics.title: Overview of the UK's human landscape

outcomes.text: Describe differences between urban core and rural areas and how UK and EU policies tried to reduce them.
Explain how migration over the past 50 years changed the UK's population and diversity.
Explain how changes in economic sectors altered employment in contrasting UK regions.
Explain how globalisation, free trade and privatisation increased foreign direct investment and the role of TNCs.
Explain the chosen UK city's site, situation and connectivity in national, regional and global context.
Describe the city's structure by function, building age, density, land use and environmental quality.

subtopics.title: People and inequality in the city

outcomes.text: Explain how migration shapes the growth and character of different parts of the city.
Explain reasons for inequality in employment, services, education and health across the city.

subtopics.title: Decline and growth in the city

outcomes.text: Explain how parts of the city have declined through de-industrialisation, decentralisation and e-commerce.
Explain how parts of the city have grown through sprawl, business services, investment and gentrification.
Evaluate the positive and negative impacts of regeneration and rebranding on people.
Describe strategies for more sustainable urban living and better quality of life.
Explain how the city and nearby rural areas are interdependent, with costs and benefits for both.
Explain why a rural area has changed economically and socially through links to the city.
Describe rural challenges: housing, primary job decline, healthcare and education, and their effect on quality of life.
Evaluate rural diversification and tourism as new income sources and their environmental impacts.
Formulate enquiry questions for investigating the effects of coastal management on processes and communities.
Choose fieldwork methods: a quantitative method on beach and sediment change and a qualitative method on management success.
Use a geology map and one other secondary source for a coastal investigation.
Formulate enquiry questions on how drainage basin and channel characteristics affect flood risk.
Choose fieldwork methods: a quantitative channel measure and a qualitative method on flood-risk factors.
Use a flood risk map and one other secondary source for a river investigation.
Formulate enquiry questions on how and why quality of life varies within urban areas.
Choose fieldwork methods: a qualitative method on perceptions and a quantitative method on environmental quality.
Use census data and one other secondary source for an urban investigation.
Formulate enquiry questions on how and why deprivation varies within rural areas.
Choose fieldwork methods: a qualitative method on rural life perceptions and a quantitative method on environmental quality.
Use census data and one other secondary source for a rural investigation.
Understand the questions fieldwork can investigate and the enquiry process, and the range of fieldwork techniques.
Process and present fieldwork data using maps, GIS, graphs and diagrams.
Analyse and explain fieldwork data using case studies and theories, and draw evidenced conclusions.
Reflect critically on fieldwork data, methods, conclusions and knowledge gained.

topics.title: Global biomes and the importance of the biosphere

outcomes.text: Explain how climate influences the distribution and characteristics of the major biomes.
Explain how local factors alter biome distribution and how living and non-living components interact.
Describe the goods the biosphere provides for local people and how it is exploited commercially.
Explain how the biosphere regulates the atmosphere, soil health and the water cycle.
Explain trends raising demand for food, energy and water and the Malthus and Boserup theories.
Explain how the rainforest's living and non-living parts are interdependent and how plants and animals adapt.
Explain why rainforests cycle nutrients quickly, supporting high biodiversity and complex food webs.
Explain how the taiga's living and non-living parts are interdependent and how plants and animals adapt.
Explain why the taiga has lower productivity, slower nutrient cycling and less biodiversity.
Explain the causes of rainforest deforestation: logging, farming, fuelwood, biofuels, minerals and HEP.
Explain why climate change is an indirect threat to rainforests.
Describe direct and indirect threats to the taiga from logging, minerals, fossil fuels and HEP.
Explain how acid precipitation, fires, pests and disease reduce taiga biodiversity.
Evaluate global actions like CITES and REDD for protecting rainforest, and why deforestation rates vary.
Explain the challenge of sustainable forest management and how alternative livelihoods might protect rainforest.
Describe the challenges of protected wilderness areas, national parks and sustainable forestry in the taiga.
Explain conflicting views on protecting or exploiting taiga resources.

subtopics.title: Types of energy and their impacts

outcomes.text: Classify energy resources as non-renewable, renewable or recyclable.
Describe the environmental impacts of mining and drilling and the landscape impacts of renewable energy.
Explain how technology and physical resources affect access to energy.
Describe the global pattern of energy use per capita and the causes of variation.
Explain the uneven distribution of oil and why oil consumption is growing.
Explain how conflict, diplomacy and economic cycles affect oil supply and prices.
Evaluate the economic benefits and costs of new conventional oil and gas in sensitive, isolated areas.
Evaluate the environmental costs of unconventional oil and gas such as tar sands and shale gas.
Explain how energy efficiency and conservation reduce demand and carbon emissions.
Evaluate the costs and benefits of biofuels, wind, solar, HEP and hydrogen as alternatives.
Explain how consumers, TNCs, governments, scientists and environmental groups hold contrasting views on energy futures.
Explain how affluence, environmental concern and education change energy attitudes in some developed countries.
Describe patterns of human and physical features using maps, atlases and sketch maps.
Describe and identify the site, situation and shape of settlements.
Interpret diagrams, graphs, sketches and aerial, oblique, ground and satellite photographs.
Use online census sources to get population and local data.
Use gradient, contour, spot height, cross sections, coordinates, scale and GIS data.
Select, construct and interpret bar charts, pie charts, line charts, histograms, population pyramids and flow-line maps.
Develop hypotheses and key questions, choose sampling methods and sample sizes, and assess risks.
Design data collection sheets and select methods to ensure accuracy and reliability.
Calculate mean, median, mode, range, quartiles and percentage change.
Describe bivariate relationships using scatter plots, lines of best fit, and interpolation and extrapolation.
Spot weaknesses in selective statistical presentation and draw evidenced conclusions.
